title: Pick This Wrong and You Could Blow Your Deal
content: My father-in-law is a farmer. This is one of his peach trees. And he says that when you're pruning a peach tree, you want gaps big enough in the peach tree that you can throw a chicken through them. And I don't know if that's just him or that's a thing that people say a lot. But it makes me think about business. And the profit margin you're looking for when you're looking at a accounting firm usually cuz that's primarily what I deal with. But when you're looking Oh gosh, that might have been a chicken. Oh, that's probably why. Maybe they used to have chickens. Anyways, when you're looking at a firm and you're looking at buying it, a lot of times people are throwing around two basic accounts of what the general profit is. One is SDE, sellers discretionary earnings, and one is IBIDA. IBIDA is often used in bigger companies. Sellers discretionary earnings is more commonly used in a situation where you have like one owner operator and another owner operator is coming to the equation um to replace the initial one. So that owner operator in that context just means somebody who owns the business is also doing the work and running it dayto-day. So SDE seller's discretionary earnings is a perfect thing to be considered when you're stepping into the shoes of the seller. So if I'm one buyer and buying a 100% owned company, I am going to replace the seller with myself. I can say, well, what did that guy bring home or girl? Right? Like would they pay themselves? What's their self-employment IRA look like? Do they run their vehicle through the company? you know, do they pay their son and then I can, you know, put know that I'll get that money back. You know, there's a million different ways that people wind up actually compensating themselves when they're running a company. And all of those I step into the shoes of if I'm the subsequent owner operator. So, solar discretionary earnings makes a ton of sense. IBIDA is more of a function that you would use if you're not going to operate the company. So if you have to take that owner operator who was doing all those things and replace them with just somebody who costs $150,000 a year, then you know that what's left is the IBIDA. It can be really hard. That sounds so simple, right? You just replace the owner operator with somebody who costs $150,000 a year. That is super challenging in practice because people don't really run businesses like an owner unless they are an owner. So having somebody who can replace an owner usually takes more than one person in my experience. Uh if you're replacing one owner operator with the other, seller discretionary earnings makes sense. If you're buying a business, you've already got a job and you're running it fully as a investment vehicle. You're going to be managing it remotely while everybody else does the work. That's more of an EVA consideration. Where it gets tricky is where you have three owner operators and one person buying it. So you kind of want to back out. Usually for SDE analysis, you're trying to normalize for one owner operator. So you would in that instance you would back out the salary for one of the three partners and kind of do a hybrid adjusted IBIDA for that. That's how those are typically used in my world to evaluate the profit of a company and it's mostly perspective. It's mostly saying how do I figure out how much money I'm going to make as the owner of this company. And ultimately that's usually what matters to the buyer. So I'm Sarah Sharp. If you found this valuable please engage with the content. Go check out dealacademy.org. forward.
description:
What’s the difference between SDE (Seller’s Discretionary Earnings) and EBITDA—and why does it matter when you’re buying a business?

Think of it like pruning a peach tree (yes, really). There should be enough gaps to throw a chicken through… and when you’re evaluating an accounting firm, you need to know which “gaps” in the numbers actually matter to you as the buyer.

In this video, I break down:
✔️ When to use SDE vs EBITDA in small business deals
✔️ Why owner-operators should care about SDE
✔️ Why investors and absentee owners focus on EBITDA
✔️ The tricky math when multiple partners are involved
✔️ How to figure out what you’ll actually take home as the new owner

If you’re buying (or selling) an accounting firm—or any small business—you need to understand these metrics before you sign an LOI.
